paper_title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

The code and model weights will be publicly released. 1. Introduction proactive assistant watches person cook, assemble or repair through head-mounted camera, and must decide every few seconds whether the current step is complete and whether something has gone wrong [10, 11, 39, 53]. Speaking at the wrong moment is costly in both directions: premature done sends the person on to step they are not ready for, and false alarm interrupts work that was going wellthe moment of an interruption changes how much it costs [1], and false or repeated alerts make people less likely to act on the next one [3, 20]. The promise of video language models is that these decisions can be read off the scene. We find that one can score well on current benchmarks without reading the scene at all. Consider rule that never looks at the video: 25 into every step it raises an alarm, and at 30 it declares the step complete. On Ego-MCBench [11] this rule reaches mistake F1 of 0.373, above every result reported for the benchmark (at most 0.27). It confirms no step in time, but such rules trade alarms against confirmations along whole curve, and with learned policy on the same inputs they trace frontier that every reported per-step result lies on or below (Fig. 2; the revised scores of the benchmark paper in Supplement B). We call this curve the video-blind frontier (Sec. 3): the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 reached by timing rules and learned policy that see the elapsed time, the instruction and training-set statistics, but never the frames. It contains all twelve zero-shot models that we evaluate on the Qualcomm Interactive Cooking dataset (QICD) [10], from 2B models to Qwen3.8-Max, and frontier of the same kind contains the speaking-time results published on GuideMe [39]. The clock does not score because elapsed time predicts single checkits AUROC is 0.52but because the protocol accepts the first confirmation within tolerance window, annotations cluster at step boundaries, and the typical duration of each instruction can be learned from the training split. Models end up inside the frontier because the protocol asks every 5 and one alarm voids step: in 83% of the steps in which zero-shot Qwen3VL-2B raises false alarm, it does so at the very first check, it and Qwen3.8-Max lose more than half of the mistake-free steps to false alarms, and plainly fine-tuned models confirm steps before they end. Both failures happen at moments when time has passed and the evidence has not yet arrived. Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT, Sec. 4) puts these moments into training. It fine-tunes the model on the protocols own checks and pairs positives with negatives from another step of the same recording at the same elapsed time  (Fig. 1)  . The pair shares the kitchen, the person and the elapsed time, so elapsed time cannot separate its two sides. The recipe is simple; its effect is not. 2B model trained with ECT on 209 videos, in about 15 GPU-hours and with neither synthetic data nor decision threshold, lies beyond the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds, and does so on held-out halves of the test set with probability 0.87 0.97 on QICD and 0.991.00 on Ego-MC-Bench (Sec. 5). On Ego-MC-Bench, on which it is never trained, it confirms 59.0% of the mistake-free steps in time, against 30.4% for the same backbone fine-tuned on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains (Sec. 6). At equal elapsed time it ranks finished step above an unfinished one in 9092% of test pairs, where elapsed time alone scores 50% and the instructions typical duration 65%. Rescaling the time stamps written between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, but costs the models trained without paired negatives, and model trained on black frames, much of their separation. Swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, drops its completion accuracy from 41.2 to 13.4. The paired negatives work by cutting the share of checks that raise false alarm from 18% to 7%, which accounts for most of the gain in completion accuracy. Our contributions are: diagnosis and tool. We show that results on two guidance benchmarks can be matched without the video, formalize this as the video-blind frontier, explain why the clock scores, and recommend reporting this margin. simple method. ECT supervises the protocols own checks and pairs positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, with no synthetic data and no decision threshold. Evidence. 2B model trained with ECT lies beyond the frontier on both benchmarks. Time-matched pairs, rescaled time stamps and video swaps show that its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains, and replay of its decisions shows that paired negatives work mainly by cutting false alarms at each check. 2. Related Work Interactive guidance. Building on large egocentric video datasets [18, 25], HoloAssist [53] recorded instructors guiding people through manual tasks and observed that instructors step in at once for critical mistakes. QICD [10], built on CaptainCook4D [41], turned live cooking guidance into benchmark that scores completion feedback and mistake feedback together; Ego-MC-Bench [11] added recordings in which human coach gives feedback in real time, and model fine-tuned on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals; GuideMe [39] extends closed-loop guidance to several domains. Offline, expert feedback can be generated or retrieved for recorded attempt [4, 5]. We evaluate on the first two under their official protocol and re-read their published results against policies that do not see the video. 2 Figure 2. The video-blind frontier contains every published Ego-MC-Bench result and every zero-shot model we run on QICD; ECT lies beyond it on both benchmarks in all four seeds. The gray region is reached by policies that use only the elapsed time, the instruction and training-set statistics: timing rules and learned policy, both tuned on the test set itself. Points are scores under the per-step protocol; published points are the 18 per-step results of Ego-MC-Bench v2, and its v3 results also lie inside. On Ego-MC-Bench single rule (black cross) has higher mistake F1 than every published result, at zero completion accuracy; Qwen3.8-Max is the only zero-shot model beyond the frontier there. When to speak. Streaming videolanguage models process video as it arrives [16] and decide at every frame or chunk whether to respond [15, 43]; benchmarks now score the timing of proactive responses [55, 63], and Chatterjee et al. [14] show that protocols that pause to ask hide the cost of late and missing responses. In several learned systems the decision is governed by parameter that sets how often the model speaks: threshold on silence token [15, 37, 62], perplexity gate [61], an activation threshold [51], or thresholds on dedicated heads and reward weights [54, 56, 59]. Others decide with learned gate [19], trained trigger model [64] or planning agent [60]. Recent assistants tie speaking to the visual state of the task, through an explicit plan [33], memory [23] or learned speak decisions [32, 58], and streaming question answering does so with completion checks [26] or readiness head trained with paired moments [6]; ProMemAssist [42] instead times its messages from model of the users working memory. We share that goal; we add no separate decision module, but change the training distribution so that elapsed time cannot explain the labels, and test whether the resulting timing depends on the video. put. We ask whether the moment to speak can, and because the answer depends on two coupled metrics we give frontier rather than single baseline. Umapathi [49] notes that degenerate speaking policies score well on macro-F1. The closest precedent is PROVIA [57], which requires online mistake detectors to beat perception-free controls built from the step index, the elapsed time and priors; we carry this idea over to interactive guidance. Concurrently, Ben-Ami et al. [9] show with clock baseline that elapsed time is shortcut for whether enough evidence has been seen in streaming question answering when negatives are sampled only before the evidence. We study the sequential protocol of guidance benchmarks, intervene on the video at the level of the models decisions, and train model that moves beyond the frontier. Our pairs hold the recording and the elapsed time fixed, so the cue they remove is the clock, and we use them both to train the model and to test it. Shortcuts and complementary pairs. Balanced pairs and changed answer priors exposed language shortcuts in visual question answering [2, 24], and minimal pairs probe compositionality [47] and visual grounding [48]; single well-chosen frame answers much of video question answering [13], many multimodal benchmark items can be answered without the image [17], and time-reversed negatives teach models temporal order [7]. These works ask whether the answer can be obtained without the intended visual inProcedural mistake detection. separate line of work builds datasets of mistakes in recorded procedures [28, 34, 41, 45] and detects or attributes them, offline [27, 31, 38, 40] or online [22, 44], surveyed by Li et al. [36]. Spurio et al. [46] post-train visionlanguage model on pairs with the same step description and opposite evidence, for offline detection. These methods score segments or actions; none is evaluated on confirming completion and flagging mistakes together under given instruction, where every alarm is weighed against confirmation. 3 3. Do the benchmarks reward seeing? The video-blind frontier that blind policy does at least as well on both metrics. To favor the blind policies, we tune them on the test set itself. On the two benchmarks we study, most reported scores can be reached without looking at the video. Protocol and metrics. We use the official per-step protocol of QICD [10] and Ego-MC-Bench [11]. On QICD we use the Advanced Planning set, where the two decisions constrain each other most: its test split contains only recordings that deviate from the plan, and half of its steps contain mistake. The model is given the current steps instruction, and the input window is anchored at that steps annotated start. Only model confirmation advances the instruction; if step is never confirmed, later steps are not reached (Supplement A). Every 5 it receives the frames observed since the step began (at most 240) and is asked, with the official prompts and greedy decoding, whether the step is complete and, if not, whether mistake has occurred; an answer is positive under the official parsing rule (it contains yes). We call each such query check. In this protocol, zeroshot Qwen3-VL-2B denotes the stronger of its two variants, with the memory prompt of Bhattacharyya et al. [11], unless stated otherwise. Completion accuracy (IC-Acc) is the share of mistake-free steps whose completion is confirmed within 15 of the annotated step end; any mistake feedback issued during such step voids it. Mistake F1 matches mistake feedback to annotated mistakes with the same 15 tolerance. The two metrics are coupled: every alarm can void step that would otherwise count, and model that never raises an alarm protects its completion accuracy at mistake F1 of zero. Neither number can be read alone. The video-blind frontier. video-blind policy decides when to confirm and when to raise an alarm from the time elapsed since the step began, the step index, the instruction text and statistics of the training split, and never from the frames. We consider three families of rules: fixed delays (confirm completion seconds into every step, raise one alarm at seconds); confirmation at multiple of the typical duration of the same instruction in the training split; and alarms only for instructions that often go wrong in the training split. We add learned policy on the same inputs: gradient-boosted trees fit on the QICD training and validation splits predict each steps duration and mistake probability, and grid of policies confirms and alarms at multiples of the predicted duration. We run every rule, per-step mixtures of rules and every learned policy through the official scorer, and define the video-blind frontier as the upper convex hull of the resulting (IC-Acc, F1) points  (Fig. 2)  . The margin of result is its mistake F1 minus the frontiers F1 at the same or higher IC-Acc; negative margin means Comparing reported results with the frontier. single ruleraise an alarm 25 into every step and confirm completion at 30 sreaches mistake F1 of 0.373 on EgoMC-Bench, above every reported result (at most 0.27); with its two delays chosen on the QICD validation split instead, it still reaches 0.361. This rule confirms no step in time, which is why the comparison is made along the frontier. None of the 18 per-step results in Tables 2 and 3 of EgoMC-Bench [11] lies beyond the frontier, in either version of that paper (Supplement B); the result with the highest mistake F1 (33.0 / 0.27, fine-tuned Qwen3.5-2B in v3) has = 0.054. The pattern is not specific to these benchmarks: on the speaking-time metrics of GuideMe [39], all 13 results of the main table lie inside or on frontier built from blind timing rules, and never speaking matches or exceeds 11 of them (Supplement B). Evaluating zero-shot models. Under the same protocol, all twelve zero-shot models that we run on QICD lie inside the frontier (Fig. 2, Tab. 1): six models with 2B to 8B parameters from three families, four sizes of Qwen3.5 from 27B to 397B, and two Qwen3.8 models. Larger models are not reliably better here (the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 models are given 16 frames per check), and most of the small models never raise an alarm. On Ego-MC-Bench only Qwen3.8Max crosses the frontier (37.9 / 0.324, = +0.025). Why the clock scores. The reason is not that elapsed time predicts the answer to an individual check: over the checks of the QICD test set its area under the ROC curve (AUROC) is about 0.52 for either question. The clock scores because the protocol is sequential. The first confirmation ends step and is accepted within 15 s, so rule only has to choose when to speak first, not to be right at every check. And the annotations sit where clock can find them: 91% of the mistake feedback in QICD is annotated exactly at the end of the step. Where recipes repeat, as in QICD, the training split adds the typical duration of each instruction: relative to it, elapsed time separates completions at an AUROC of 0.61, signal that fine-tuning on the protocols checks can pick up. On Ego-MC-Bench only 2 of 562 instructions occur in the training split (Supplement B). Two ways to end up inside. We recommend reporting the margin over the video-blind frontier alongside results on these benchmarks; Supplement lists its vertices. 4. Evidence-Contrastive Training Both failures in Sec. 3 occur at moments when time has passed and the evidence has not arrived. EvidenceContrastive Training (ECT) puts these moments into training. It has two ingredients: each training example is check of the benchmark protocol, and positives are paired with negatives at the same elapsed time. Situations. Every training example is one check of the protocol, which we call situation: the frames since the step began, the official prompt, and the answer. From the QICD annotations we take mistake situations at the annotated feedback time and 5 and 10 later, answered YES followed by the feedback, and success situations at the step end and 5 later, answered YES. Checks at which nothing should be said are answered NO; these include checks placed before an annotated mistake, outside its tolerance window. During training, situations are sampled by kind with fixed weights (Supplement J). Paired negatives. For positive at elapsed time E, ECT looks for negative from another step of the same recording at the same (Fig. 1 shows one such pair); we call these paired negatives. notdone negative pairs success situation with step that still has at least 20 to run, and answers NO to the completion question; it targets early confirmation. clean negative pairs mistake situation with mistake-free step that still has at least 15 to run, and answers NO to the mistake question; it targets alarms without evidence. Not every positive has such partner in its recording: we obtain 4,068 notdone negatives for 4,563 success situations and 1,159 clean negatives for 1,938 mistake situations. What the pair controls. Because both sides come from one recording, the kitchen, the person and the camera are shared; because the elapsed time is equal, so are the window length and the clock reading. Within pair, any policy that reads only the elapsed time or the window length must give both sides the same answer; the instruction can still differ, and with it the steps typical duration. Pooled over all positives and their paired negatives, elapsed time separates the labels with an AUROC of 0.541 for the completion question and 0.606 for the mistake question, since not every positive has partner. Training and inference. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-2B [8] with rank-64 LoRA [30] for 2,400 steps, about one epoch over the roughly 18,400 situations built from the 209 training videos, with cross-entropy on the answer tokens; this takes about 15 GPU-hours on single A100-40G. At test time the model is run exactly as in Sec. 3: the official prompts and greedy decoding. ECT uses no decision threshold and no synthetic data. 5. Results Setup. ECT is trained on the 209 training videos of QICD Advanced Planning and evaluated on its 36 test videos and, without any adaptation, on the 39 available videos of EgoMC-Bench. The two benchmarks are complementary: in QICD mistake feedback is almost always annotated at the end of step, whereas in Ego-MC-Bench human coach gives it while the step is under way (4% at the step end). Each test configuration is run once. We train four seeds, report the mean and standard deviation over seeds, and test differences with paired bootstrap over videos [21] and Holm correction [29]. ECT lies beyond the frontier. All four seeds lie beyond the video-blind frontier on both benchmarks (Tab. 1, Fig. 2). On QICD, ECT reaches 40.81.3 IC-Acc and 0.2470.033 mistake F1, with margins from +0.012 to +0.061; on EgoMC-Bench, on which it is never trained, 59.0 5.7 and 0.246 0.034, with margins from +0.17 to +0.28. Two of the Ego-MC-Bench seeds exceed the completion accuracy of every blind policy, where the frontier is zero; the other two have margins of +0.169 and +0.259 against non-zero frontier. The pre-registered variant with decision thresholds chosen on validation data is also beyond the frontier in every seed (Tab. 1). When the blind policies are tuned on one half of the test videos and the margin is measured on the other, seed lies beyond the frontier in 8797% of 500 splits on QICD and 99100% on Ego-MC-Bench (Supplement B). Against published fine-tuned models. ECT uses 209 QICD videos and 2,400 steps on one A100, versus about 100k iterations on eight H100 GPUs for the reported same-backbone model. Qwen3-VL writes time stamp between the frames of window. On 411 fixed validation checks we doubled or halved every stamp, keeping the pixels, the number of frames and the prompt (Supplement H). ECT (seed 0) is unaffected: its AUROC is 0.945, 0.942 and 0.943 for completion and 0.841, 0.820 and 0.846 for mistakes with the original, doubled and halved stamps. Without paired negatives, the same check separates mistakes from silence at 0.971 with the original stamps and 0.790.80 with rescaled ones, no longer above ECT; both rescalings raise its probability of yes on silent checks, so it reacts to unfamiliar stamps rather than reading their value. After plain finetuning the separation drops from 0.961 to 0.600.61. The ECT recipe trained on black frames separates completions at 0.920 without any video, and 0.740.77 once the stamps are rescaled. ECT still uses how long step usually takes, as coach would: its confirmation times follow the median training duration of the instruction, cue its training pairs leave in place. At equal elapsed time, though, it scores 0.900.92 on the pairs where this cue reaches 0.65 and the black-frame model 0.620.64. What the negatives change. Fine-tuning on the protocols checks improves completion accuracy; the paired negatives change the balance between confirmations and alarms (Tab. 2). Fine-tuning without paired negatives already puts the model beyond the frontier on Ego-MC-Bench ( = +0.139); on QICD it stays inside ( = 0.066). It gets there by raising alarms without evidence: 48% of the mistake-free steps are voided, with 1.31.5 false alarms per mistake-free step (0.50.6 for ECT), and completion accuracy on QICD is 26.5. Clean negatives halve the voided steps (25%) and lift completion accuracy to 43.3, with the largest margin on QICD. Re-balancing the answers by sampling, instead of adding negatives, keeps the completion accuracy low and the false alarms in place. Notdone negatives make the confirmation follow the progress of the step: on the unseen steps of Ego-MC-Bench its correlation with the steps duration is 0.450.69 for the variants trained with them (0.68 with notdone negatives alone), 0.300.40 for those without and 0.10 for the zeroshot model, and fewer mistake-free steps are confirmed more than 15 early (3755 against 6282; Supplement C). Negatives drawn at random moments of the same steps also put both tested seeds beyond the frontier on both benchmarks: within recording the clock separates them from the positives about as poorly as matched ones (AUROC 0.5550.561 and 0.6070.620, against 0.541 and 0.606), and they shift the trade-off between the two metrics (Supplement C). Where the gain comes from. For ECT and the variant without paired negatives (seed 0 of each), we logged both probabilities at every check of the QICD test set and replayed the official protocol offline; at the thresholds of the pre-registered decoding the replay matches the official ICAcc of both runs (42.0 and 31.1), counting the few steps 8 that outlast the log as confirmed at the next check (Supplement F). Over the checks of mistake-free steps, 7.3% raise false alarm for ECT and 18.3% for the variant, and 26.5% and 40.8% of these steps are voided. Giving the variant the mistake probabilities of ECT, with its own completion probabilities, raises its IC-Acc from 31.1 to 40.8, close to the 42.0 of ECT (23.1 to 38.7 against 39.1 at thresholds of 0.5, the closest to greedy decoding): fewer false alarms per check account for most of the gain in completion accuracy. The completion side improves too: with every alarm removed, ECT confirms more steps in time than the variant at every completion threshold from 0.1 to 0.6 (at best 61.3 against 54.6). The operating point. The negatives trade mistake recall for confirmations: without them mistake F1 on Ego-MCBench is higher (0.34) at completion accuracy 11 points lower, because the model raises alarms in about twice as many steps, at precision of 0.33 against 0.43 (Supplement C), and tripling the clean negatives moves QICD from 40.8 / 0.247 to 52.5 / 0.222. How many negatives to use is therefore choice of operating point. Given the same validation cap of 432 raw alarms, the two variants without clean negatives fall 7.1 and 5.9 completion points short of thresholded ECT on QICD (Supplement D). 7. Limitations and Conclusion Limitations. Our study covers cooking, two benchmarks and their official protocol, and Ego-MC-Bench is evaluated by transfer. blind learner with more inputs than our definition allows can extend the frontier: one that also sees the durations of the earlier steps of the same recording, which the protocol reveals, brings the QICD margins of greedy ECT to 0.028+0.029, while those on Ego-MC-Bench and the QICD Main set stay positive (Supplement B). ECT improves the timing of what the model says more than the mistakes it catches: its mistake recall stays low (0.18 on Ego-MC-Bench), it separates mistakes from mistake-free completions at step end less well than fine-tuning without paired negatives (Supplement E), and detection is credited by its time alone. In manual check of 25 detections, 9 named the annotated mistake, 3 named it in part, and 13 named different one (Supplement G). Conclusion. Under their per-step protocol, two benchmarks for proactive guidance currently reward the clock, and the video-blind frontier measures by how much. ECT moves 2B model beyond it on both benchmarks without synthetic data or decision threshold. At equal elapsed time its decisions are set by the video, it ignores the time stamps that blind model relies on, and its paired negatives work by cutting false alarms at each check. We recommend reporting the margin over the frontier with every result on these benchmarks.

sections.content: Paired negatives change when ECT responds: under the official protocol, it confirms steps on time more often and raises fewer false alarms, at the cost of some mistake recall. Reading guide. Appendices and ask how much stalling and video-blind timing can explain. Appendices and compare the training variants and decoding choices. Appendices to examine individual decisions, feedback and video perturbations. Appendix describes the scope of the public materials. The main paper and supplement share one list of references. Analyses marked were designed after the test results; they change no reported model or main result, and Appendix lists the use of the test sets in order. A. Protocol, models and settings Protocol. We use the official per-step evaluation loop and scorer for both benchmarks. Inference settings and any changes to prompting or answer parsing are described below. The model is given the ground-truth instruction of the current step; check is made every 10 frames (5 at 2 frames per second) on the frames since the annotated start, at most 240 (120 s). In the protocol described in Sec. 3, the annotated start anchors the window, but only model confirmation advances the instruction. If step is never confirmed, the model keeps being checked on later footage under that instruction and subsequent steps are never reached. In four audited runs on the 36 QICD test recordings, the number of instructions issued equaled the number of confirmations plus one, capped at the number of steps. At each check the completion question is asked first and, if the answer is negative, the mistake question. An answer is positive if it contains yes; our fine-tuned models answer YES or NO at the start of the output, so the rule is unambiguous for them. mistake-free step contributes an IC hit only if its single prediction is confirmation within the 15 tolerance of the annotated step end; any mistake feedback during the step voids the hit. Unreached mistakefree steps remain in the denominator. The memory prompt is the one-minute feedback memory of Bhattacharyya et al. [11]; in our runs the memory is cleared at every step. Of the 40 sessions of Ego-MC-Bench, 39 are released (562 instructions, 397 mistake annotations); the published results use 40. Stalling and how failed steps are annotated. The two benchmarks annotate step with mistake differently. In QICD Advanced Planning, 236 of the 474 test steps contain mistake and none of them carries an annotated success: the next step begins after the mistake, in 65 cases with the same instruction. In Ego-MC-Bench, 282 of the 298 steps with mistake end with success after the correction, and 16 (3% of all steps) end with the mistake. Since only confirmation advances the instruction, model that withholds confirmation on failed QICD step stays on it. Among the recordings that run leaves before the last step, the step where it stops ends with mistake in 7 of 14 for zero-shot Qwen3-VL-2B on QICD, 11 of 24 for Qwen3.5-397B and 27 of 36 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B; on Ego-MC-Bench the same models stop at such step in 0 of 5, 0 of 16 and 1 of 38 recordings, and otherwise at mistake-free step or after corrected mistake. The greedy ECT seeds stop early in 0 4 recordings per test set. Recomputing the IC denominator over the mistake-free steps each run reaches, with the official numerator, zero-shot Qwen3-VL-2B with the memory prompt reaches 385/474 steps on QICD and its IC rises from 10.5 to 13.5; Qwen3.5-397B rises from 18.1 to 28.7 on QICD and from 34.5 to 46.9 on Ego-MC-Bench; no greedy ECT seed changes by more than two points. Zeroshot Qwen2.5-VL-7B reaches only 96/562 steps on EgoMC-Bench, and its IC on that subset is 58.3 against 8.0 officially. Stalling thus explains part of the official gap of the zero-shot models, and not the low IC of the main zero-shot reference. Each reached-only IC conditions on modelspecific subset; the counts are released with the code. Zero-shot models. Table S1 lists every zero-shot run. InternVL3.5 [52] and LLaVA-OneVision [35] receive 32 frames sampled uniformly from the window, zero-shot and fine-tuned alike. The Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 models are run through hosted inference service with 16 frames per check (448 pixels wide, with time stamps), the memory prompt, temperature 0 and reasoning disabled. For these models we append Start your answer with YES or NO, then give at most one sentence. to the question and parse only the leading word, because without the suffix some answers contain yes mid-sentence. Requests rejected by the services content filter are counted as NO; this affects at most 108 checks per model on QICD and none on EgoMC-Bench. Two models were accidentally queried twice: the decisions of the two passes agree in 99.9100% of the checks. With these settings Qwen3.5-27B reaches 42.0 / 0.068 on Ego-MC-Bench, below the 45.5 / 0.14 published for it with its own settings [11]; the paper uses the published value when it discusses published results. The zero-shot conclusion does not depend on greedy decoding: with sampling, Qwen3-VL-2B reaches 5.5 / 0.099, 3.8 / 0.103 and 2.9 / 0.102 on QICD over three seeds.

The rules use the step start, the elapsed time, the instruction text and statistics of the QICD training split. (ii) Duration priors: confirm at multiple of the median training duration of the same instruction (the global median if the instruction is unseen). Both lie inside the frontier and react little to black frames. Forced to answer, the two systems thus sit near the two blind extremes of the paper: alarms regardless of the video, and silence. J. Training data and recipe Situations. From the 209 training videos we build 18,406 situations (seed 0): 1,938 mistake, 4,563 success, 6,315 silence, 363 shifted, 4,068 notdone and 1,159 clean. Mistake situations are placed at the annotated feedback time and 5 and 10 later, success situations at the step end and 5 later, and silence situations every 20 inside step, away from any annotated event. shifted situation is check before an annotated mistake and outside its tolerance window, answered NO. Each training step draws 8 situations by kind with fixed weights: mistake 0.25, success 0.20, silence, notdone and clean 0.15 each, and shifted 0.10. Optimization. We train LoRA adapters of rank 64 on Qwen3-VL-2B with AdamW, learning rate of 2 104 and cross-entropy on the answer tokens for 2,400 steps (19,200 situations, about one epoch). run takes about 15 hours on one A100: five later runs of the same pipeline took 13.616.8 hours; the four seeds of ECT shared their GPUs with other jobs and took 18.028.6 hours of wall-clock time, seed 3 on an A100-80GB (peak memory 9.1 GiB). Seed 0 of + notdone was interrupted and resumed from its checkpoint at step 2,300. The three controls. The rows of the ablation differ from ECT as follows. No paired negatives differs in the negatives alone: the situations are built in the same way, the notdone and clean situations are removed, and the weights of the remaining kinds are renormalized (mistake 0.36, success 0.29, silence 0.21, shifted 0.14). No negatives, rebalanced sampling uses the same situations as the previous variant with other weights (silence 0.40, success 0.25, mistake 0.25, shifted 0.10), which brings the share of YES answers to the mistake question close to that of ECT. Plain fine-tuning is an earlier recipe and differs in four ways: one mistake situation per annotated mistake and one success situation per step (9,632 situations: 6,315 silence, 2,303 success, 652 mistake, 362 shifted); uniform sampling over situations, so that mistakes make up about 7% of the draws; the other question asked on 30% of the positive situations instead of 20%; and no paired negatives. It is trained for two epochs (2,408 steps) with the same model and optimizer. With so few positive examples for the mistake question it learns never to raise an alarm, which under the official scoring voids no step and gives it the highest completion accuracy; the gap between it and ECT cannot be attributed to the negatives. Splits and shortcuts. The training, validation and test videos of QICD Advanced Planning (209, 57 and 36) are disjoint, and Ego-MC-Bench was recorded separately.
